code.title: Global, function, block and module scope with shadowing

followUps:
Yes, the catch (e) parameter is block-scoped: it exists only inside the catch block and disappears afterwards. It behaves like a let declared at the top of that block, so typeof e after the block gives "undefined".

One oddity: a var e inside the catch block is still allowed in sloppy mode, but it is hoisted to the function and the assignment goes to the parameter. Avoid it.

A top-level let in a classic script lives in the global declarative scope: every script can see it by name, but it does not become a property of window. A top-level var does become a property.

var a = 1; let b = 2;
window.a; // 1
window.b; // undefined

In an ES module or in a Node file, top-level names are private to that file anyway.

Scope answers "which variables can I see?" and is fixed by where the code is written. this answers "which object is this call about?" and is mostly fixed by how the function is called.

Example: an arrow function takes its this from the surrounding scope, but a normal function gets it from the call (obj.f() gives obj). A variable lookup never depends on the caller, while this usually does.

code.title: var, let and const side by side

followUps:
Use Object.freeze(obj), but know that it is shallow: it blocks adding, deleting and changing the object's own properties, yet nested objects stay changeable.

For true immutability, freeze recursively:

function deepFreeze(o) {
  Object.values(o).forEach(v =>
    typeof v === 'object' && v && deepFreeze(v));
  return Object.freeze(o);
}

In strict mode, writing to a frozen object throws a TypeError; in sloppy mode it is silently ignored. Cost is O(size of the object graph).

The classic for loop runs i++, which re-assigns i, and a const cannot be re-assigned. The body runs once with i = 0, then the increment throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

for (const x of arr) works because each iteration makes a brand-new binding for x and nothing ever assigns to it again. Use let in counting loops and const in for-of loops.

code.title: Hoisting: what exists before its line runs

followUps:
Both are hoisted, and the function wins at the start, but the var's assignment wins at the end. The creation phase gives the name the function body; then when execution reaches var x = 1, the name becomes 1.

var dup = 1;
function dup() {}
typeof dup; // "number"

Without the assignment, var dup; function dup(){} leaves a function, because a bare var does not reset the value.

Yes. import declarations are hoisted: all imports are resolved and the imported modules are evaluated before any code in the importing module runs, no matter where the import line sits.

The imported names are live, read-only bindings. If the exporter has not finished evaluating (an import cycle), reading a const or class export throws a TDZ error, while a function declaration export already works.

The var inside if (false) still gets created, because var ignores blocks and is hoisted to the top of the function. It starts as undefined and the assignment never happens.

function f() {
  if (false) { var z = 1; }
  return z;     // undefined, no error
}

This is why let is safer: the same code with let z would make z unreachable outside the block.

code.title: Temporal dead zone errors

followUps: Besides plain variables, the TDZ shows up in four places: default parameters (f(a = b, b = 1) fails because b is not set yet), classes (new Foo() before class Foo), switch cases (all cases share one block, so a let in case 2 is in the TDZ if case 1 reads it), and module cycles (reading an export of a module that has not finished evaluating).

Because typeof normally never throws, people expect it to be a safe probe. For a name that does not exist at all, typeof nope gives "undefined". But for a let/const/class name that exists and is in the TDZ, it throws ReferenceError.

typeof q;   // ReferenceError
let q;

The rule: the binding exists, so the engine refuses to read it before initialisation.

code.title: A closure keeps private state alive

followUps:
Yes. Closures created in the same call share the same variables, because they all point to the one scope of that call. In makeAccount above, deposit and read both see the same balance: after deposit(50), read() returns 150.

Closures from different calls each get their own copy of the scope, so two counters from makeCounter() never interfere.

The module pattern is just a closure used on purpose: an outer function runs once, keeps its variables private, and returns an object of inner functions as the public API. Those functions are closures over the private state.

const Mod = (function () {
  let secret = 0;
  return { inc: () => ++secret };
})();

Nothing outside can reach secret; only inc can.

Technically yes, every function object remembers the scope where it was created. But we only say closure when it matters, that is, when the function uses outer variables and is used after the outer call has ended.

A top-level function that uses only globals and its own locals is not an interesting closure. Engines also skip allocating a scope if no inner function uses it.

code.title: Loop closure bug and its fixes

followUps:
With var, it still prints 3 3 3, just at different times: the callbacks fire at about 0, 1 and 2 seconds, and each one reads the single shared i, which is already 3.

With let it prints 0 at 0 s, 1 at 1 s and 2 at 2 s. The delay only changes when the callbacks run, not which variable they share.

No. A while loop with a counter declared outside it has one binding that every closure shares, so the bug is back.

let i = 0;
while (i < 3) { fns.push(() => i); i++; }
// all return 3

Only for (let ...) creates a fresh binding per iteration. To fix a while loop, declare a const j = i inside the body and capture j.

Babel rewrites it using a function that is called once per iteration, so each call has its own parameter. Roughly:

var _loop = function (i) {
  fns.push(function () { return i; });
};
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) _loop(i);

It is the IIFE fix done by the compiler. Babel only does this when a closure actually captures the loop variable.

code.title: Lexical scope versus the call stack

followUps:
Two features can change the scope at run time: sloppy-mode eval (a var declared inside eval('var q = 1') is added to the calling function's scope) and the with statement (it puts an object's properties at the front of the scope chain).

Both are forbidden in strict mode and ES modules, and both defeat engine optimisation, so avoid them.

It is stored in the function object's internal slot [[Environment]], set when the function is created (when the function expression or declaration is evaluated). On each call, the new local scope gets its outer link from that slot.

That is why a function returned from outer() still finds outer's variables: the link points to the scope where it was created, not where it is called.

code.title: Four common error messages, triggered on purpose

followUps:
Only the first one: typeof on a name that has no binding at all returns "undefined" instead of throwing x is not defined.

It cannot avoid the TDZ error (the binding exists, so typeof throws), the const assignment error, or x is not a function (typeof early would simply return "undefined" or "object", you must check before calling).

First reproduce it with the production build and source maps so the stack trace shows real file names. Find the line that reads x at module load time, then check whether that module is part of an import cycle (a tool such as madge finds cycles).

Prod differs from dev because minifiers and scope hoisting reorder or merge modules. Fix the cycle, or read the value lazily inside a function. Do not rely on build output order.

code.title: A listener list that leaks, and a bounded fix

followUps:
A detached DOM node is an element removed from the page that JavaScript still references, so the garbage collector cannot free it or its children.

A closure does this by capturing the node: const el = document.getElementById('x'); window.onclick = () => el.id;. Even after el.remove(), the click handler still holds el. Fix by removing the listener, or by capturing only the data needed (such as the id string).

A WeakMap helps when you attach extra data to an object and want it freed when the object dies: keys are held weakly, so cache.set(node, info) will not keep node alive.

It does not help when keys are strings or numbers (they cannot be keys), when you need to count or iterate the entries (no size, no iteration), or when the value itself references the key strongly, since that does not stop the leak in all engines' simple cases.

code.title: memoize with a call counter

followUps:
Use a Map's insertion order: on every hit, delete the key and set it again so it moves to the end; when the size passes the limit, delete the first key (the least recently used).

get(k){ if(!m.has(k)) return; const v=m.get(k);
  m.delete(k); m.set(k,v); return v; }
set(k,v){ m.delete(k); m.set(k,v);
  if(m.size>max) m.delete(m.keys().next().value); }

All operations are O(1) on average. Space is O(max).

useMemo remembers only the last result for one component instance, and re-computes when its dependency array changes. A general memoize stores a result for every distinct input in a cache that can grow.

Also React may throw the cached value away, so useMemo is a performance hint, not a guarantee. Example: useMemo(() => sort(list), [list]) sorts again only when list changes.

Cache the promise, not the resolved value, so two calls in flight share one request, and delete the entry if the promise rejects so errors are not cached forever.

const p = fn(...args);
cache.set(key, p);
p.catch(() => cache.delete(key));
return p;

Add a TTL if the data goes stale. Cost: one cache entry per distinct key, O(1) lookup.

code.title: A fresh binding per loop iteration

followUps:
It returns 0. The arrow function f is created in the initialiser, so it captures the very first environment, where i is 0. The loop then copies i into new environments for each iteration and increments those copies, so the first one is never changed.

This is a real corner of the spec, visible in the program above, and is why you should not create closures in the initialiser.

With const i = 0, the first iteration runs normally because the initial value is set by the declaration. At the end of the iteration, the engine copies i into a new environment and runs i++, which tries to assign to a const binding and throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

So the error appears after the first body run, not before it.

code.title: IIFE and the module pattern

followUps:
Because a statement that starts with the keyword function is parsed as a function declaration, which must have a name and cannot be called on the spot. Wrapping it in parentheses (or starting with ! or void) makes it an expression, which can be invoked immediately.

(function () { ... })();   // OK
function () { ... }();      // SyntaxError

The revealing module pattern defines all functions and variables privately in the IIFE, then returns an object that simply points to the ones you want public, using the same names as the definitions.

const M = (function () {
  function a() {}  function b() {}
  return { a };      // b stays private
})();

It reads clearly because the public API is listed in one place at the end.

code.title: Closures in one scope share a variable

followUps:
Copy the small piece of data you need into its own variable and capture that, or build the callback in a separate small function that receives only what it needs, so the large buffer is not in its scope.

function make(buf) {
  const n = buf.length;   // small copy
  return () => n;         // buf not captured
}

Also set the big variable to null when done. Memory saved: the whole buffer (for example 8 MB) can be freed.

V8 uses a Context as the general heap object for captured variables of a scope. A FunctionContext is the one created when a function is entered, holding its captured parameters and vars. A BlockContext is created for a block that has captured let/const variables (for example a loop body whose closure captures i).

Each context links to its parent, forming the chain that closures walk. Scopes with no captured variables get no context at all.

code.title: Module-level TDZ in a cycle, simulated in one file

followUps:
A function declaration is initialised with its full body at the start of the module, before any code runs, so an importer can call it even while the exporter is still evaluating. A class (and let/const) is only initialised when its line runs, so before that it is in the TDZ.

That is why a cycle with exported functions often works and the same cycle with exported classes crashes.

CommonJS has no TDZ. require runs the module and returns its module.exports. In a cycle, the second module gets the partial exports object of the first, with only what it has added so far, so a missing property is just undefined.

Example: if A does exports.x = 1 after requiring B, B sees a.x === undefined. Symptom: silent undefined instead of a ReferenceError.

code.title: Stale closure simulated without React

followUps:
An empty array tells React "run this effect once, after the first render". The effect's callback is created in that first render, so it closes over that render's count (0), and since the effect never re-runs, it never gets a newer closure.

Fix: add count to the array (the interval is rebuilt each tick), or use setCount(c => c + 1) which does not need count at all.

Signals-based frameworks (Solid, Preact signals, Vue refs) keep state in an object that you read with count() or count.value at the moment you use it. The closure captures the signal, not a number, so it always reads the current value.

Also, their components run once instead of on every render, so there are no per-render closures to go stale. It is the same idea as the ref fix in the program above.
